q: 1. The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is:
explain: Surveys covering an area of more than 260 km2 are treated as geodetic surveys, where the curvature of the earth must be accounted for; below this the earth's surface is assumed to be a plane.

q: 2. The difference in the lengths of an arc and its subtended chord on the earth surface for a distance of 18.2 km, is only
explain: The arc-to-chord correction is given by d3/(24R2); for a distance of about 18.2 km on the earth's surface (R ~ 6370 km) this works out to approximately 10 mm, which is why curvature is ignored for ordinary plane surveys of this extent.

q: 3. Surveys which are carried out to depict mountains, rivers, water bodies, wooded areas and other cultural details, are known as
explain: Topographical surveys are meant to depict natural features (mountains, rivers, forests) as well as man-made (cultural) features on a map.

q: 4. Surveys which are carried out to provide a national grid of control for preparation of accurate maps of large areas, are known
explain: Geodetic surveys account for the earth's curvature and establish a nationwide network of precise control points used as a framework for all other surveys and mapping.

q: 5. The main principle of surveying is to work
options: from higher level to the lower level
from lower level to higher level
explain: Surveying always proceeds from whole to part: a rough framework of control points covering the whole area is fixed first (low accuracy tolerance), and details are then filled in with reference to it, which localizes and minimizes the accumulation of errors.

q: 6. Systematic errors are those errors
options: whose effects are cumulative and can be eliminated
explain: Systematic (cumulative) errors follow a definite mathematical or physical law, so their sign and magnitude can be determined and corrected/eliminated by applying suitable corrections.

q: 7. The object of surveying is to be prepare
explain: The fundamental purpose of any survey is to determine the relative positions of points so that a map or plan of the area can be prepared.

q: 8. While surveying a plot of land by plane tabling, the field observations
options: and plotting do not proceed simultaneously
and recorded in field books to be plotted later
explain: Plane tabling is unique among surveying methods in that field observation and plotting happen simultaneously on the table sheet in the field itself, eliminating the need for a separate field book.

q: 9. Survey plotting can be done with an accuracy of
explain: With good drafting instruments and practice, survey plotting can typically achieve an accuracy of about 0.25 mm on the plotted sheet.

q: 10. Pantagraph is used for
explain: A pantograph is a mechanical linkage instrument used to copy, enlarge, or reduce plans and drawings to a different scale.

q: 11. The branch of surveying in which both horizontal and vertical positions of a point, are determined by making instrumental observations, is known
explain: As per the book's answer key, this branch is designated 'tachemetry' (an alternate spelling of tacheometry), the surveying method that determines both horizontal and vertical positions instrumentally without chaining.

q: 12. Theory of probability is applied to
explain: The theory of probability is applied specifically to accidental (random) errors, since these follow the laws of chance, unlike systematic/cumulative errors which have a definite known cause and sign.

q: 13. Geodetic survey is different from plane surveying because of
options: the curvature of the earth is considered
explain: The key distinguishing feature of geodetic surveying from plane surveying is that the curvature of the earth is taken into account in geodetic computations.

q: 14. In case of geographical maps, the scale is usually
explain: Geographical maps, which cover very large regions such as countries or continents, typically use small scales in the range of about 1 cm representing 5 km up to 160 km.

q: 15. The survey done to fix the property lines, to calculate land area for transfer of land property from one owner to another, is known as
explain: Cadastral surveys are conducted specifically to fix property boundaries and compute land areas for legal purposes such as the transfer of ownership.

q: 16. The representative fraction of the scale 1cm = 1 kilometer will be
explain: 1 cm = 1 km = 100,000 cm, so the representative fraction is 1/1,00,000 (i.e., 1/10,00,00 in the Indian numbering format given).

q: 17. A discrepancy is the difference between
options: two measured values of the same quantity
explain: A discrepancy refers to the difference between two independently measured values of the same quantity (unlike an error, which is the difference between the measured value and the true value).

q: 18. Cadastral map is a map having
explain: Cadastral maps, which show detailed property boundaries, are drawn to a large scale for adequate accuracy and clarity of individual plots.

q: 19. Geodetic surveying is different from plane surveying because of
options: the large difference of elevations between various points
explain: Geodetic surveying differs fundamentally from plane surveying because it covers very large areas where the curvature of the earth cannot be ignored, requiring spherical (geodetic) rather than plane computations.

q: 20. When 1 cm on a map represents 10 m on the ground, the representative fraction of the scale is
explain: 1 cm = 10 m = 1000 cm, so the representative fraction is 1:1000, i.e., 1/1000.

q: 21. The representative fraction 1/2500 means that the scale is
explain: RF of 1/2500 means 1 cm on the map represents 2500 cm on the ground, which equals 25 m.

q: 22. Cross hairs in surveying telescope are fitted
options: at the centre of the telescope
in the optical center of the eye-piece
explain: Cross hairs are mounted on a diaphragm located in front of the eyepiece at the focal plane of the objective.

q: 23. The difference between the most probable value and its observed value is
explain: The residual error (or residual) is defined as the difference between the most probable value (usually the mean of observations) and any individual observed value.

q: 24. The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is
explain: As with Q1, surveys covering more than about 260 km2 must take the earth's curvature into account and are treated as geodetic surveys.

q: 25. In order to determine the natural features such as valleys, rivers, lakes etc., the surveying preferred is
explain: Topographical surveying is specifically aimed at depicting natural features of the terrain, such as valleys, rivers, and lakes.

q: 26. The surveying used to determine additional details such as boundaries of fields, is called
explain: Cadastral surveying is used to determine and record property/field boundaries and related administrative details.

q: 27. Mistakes which may produce a very serious effect upon the final results arise due to
explain: Serious mistakes in survey work generally result from a combination of human factors - inattention, inexperience, and carelessness - so all of these are valid causes.

q: 28. The fundamental principle of surveying is to work from the
explain: As established earlier, the fundamental principle of surveying is to proceed from the whole (a broad framework) down to the part (detailed measurements).

q: 29. The systematic errors which persist and have regular effects in the performance of a survey operations, are due to
explain: Systematic errors, which follow a definite mathematical/physical law and persist consistently, typically arise from a faulty (mis-calibrated or maladjusted) instrument.

q: 30. The working from whole to the part is done in surveying in order to ensure that
options: survey work is completed more quickly
errors and mistakes of one portion do not affect the remaining portion
explain: Working from whole to part localizes errors, so that any small error made in one part of the survey does not propagate and magnify across the rest of the survey area.

q: 31. The method of reversal
options: is usually directed to examine whether a certain part is truly parallel or perpendicular to another
makes the erroneous relationship between parts evident
explain: The method of reversal serves both purposes - it examines whether parts of an instrument are truly parallel/perpendicular to each other, and in doing so makes any erroneous relationship between them evident.

q: 32. When 1 cm on a map represents 10m on the ground, the representative fraction of the scale in
explain: 1 cm represents 10 m = 1000 cm, so the representative fraction is 1/1000.

q: 33. The apparent error on reversal is
explain: When an instrumental error is examined by the method of reversal, the apparent (observed) error is exactly twice the actual error present in the instrument's adjustment.

q: 34. A branch of surveying in which the horizontal and vertical distances of points are obtained by instrumental observations, is known as
explain: Tacheometric surveying is defined as the branch in which both horizontal and vertical distances are obtained rapidly through instrumental (stadia) observations, without chaining.

q: 35. The types of survey used for Geodetic survey is
explain: Geodetic surveys cover large areas and require extreme accuracy to account for earth's curvature, necessitating precise leveling methods.

q: 36. The angle between two plane mirrors of the optical square is kept
explain: The two plane mirrors of an optical square are set at exactly 45 degrees to each other to achieve the required 90-degree deflection of the sight line.

q: 37. The missing station of the ground survey can be found out with the help of
explain: A missing or unclear survey station's position can typically be identified/re-established with the help of a reference sketch made during the original fieldwork, showing its relation to nearby features.

q: 38. In order to determine the natural features such as valley, rivers, lakes etc., the surveying prepared is
explain: As in Q201, topographical surveying is used to determine and depict natural features such as valleys, rivers, and lakes.

q: 39. Which of the following can fulfill the objective of the airport survey?
explain: An airport survey requires detailed information on the characteristics of the soil, which is essential for pavement/runway design and foundation planning.

q: 40. Grid lines are parallel to
options: magnetic meridian of the central point of the grid
line representing the central true meridian of the grid
explain: In a survey grid system, all grid lines running north-south are drawn parallel to the line representing the central true meridian of the grid zone.

q: 41. The sum of the interior angles of a geometrical figure laid on the surface of the earth differs from that of the corresponding plane figure only to the extent of one second for every
explain: Due to the earth's curvature, the spherical excess in the interior angles of a figure on the earth's surface amounts to about one second of arc for every 100 sq. km of area (in this text's convention).

q: 42. Diaphragm of a surveying telescope is held inside
options: telescope at the end nearer the eye-piece
explain: The diaphragm (cross-hair ring) is mounted inside the telescope tube, positioned roughly at its mid-point between the objective and the eyepiece.

q: 43. The fundamental principle of surveying is to work from the
explain: The fundamental principle of all surveying is to work from the whole to the part, establishing a rough, accurate framework first before adding progressively finer detail within it.

q: 44. The working from whole to the part is done in surveying in order to ensure that
options: surveying work is completed more quickly
errors and mistakes of one portion do not affected the remaining portion
explain: Working from whole to part localizes errors - if a mistake occurs in a minor detail survey, it does not affect the accuracy of the main framework or other parts of the survey.

q: 45. Angular surveying in which both horizontal and vertical positions of a point are obtained by optical means is known as
explain: Tacheometry is the branch of surveying that uses a telescope with stadia hairs to determine distances and elevations without a tape.

q: 46. If L is the measured length of a base line whose elevation is h above MSL, the necessary correction to reduce the base length to MSL is
explain: The standard correction to reduce a measured base line length at elevation h to mean sea level is given by L.h/R, where R is the mean radius of the earth.

q: 47. In the surveying telescopes, cross hairs are fitted in
options: optical centre of the eye piece
explain: Cross hairs in a surveying telescope are mounted on the diaphragm, positioned within the tube nearer to the objective lens (rather than near the eyepiece).

q: 48. In the surveying telescope, diaphragm is held
explain: The diaphragm (cross-hair mounting) inside a surveying telescope's tube is positioned nearer to the objective lens than to the eyepiece.

q: 49. The principle of working from whole to part is used in surveying because
options: survey work can be completed quickly
explain: Working from whole to part serves multiple purposes together - simplifying plotting, speeding up survey work, and preventing accumulation of errors - so all of these are valid reasons.

q: 50. The type of surveying which requires least office work is
explain: Since plane table surveying involves plotting directly in the field simultaneously with observation, it requires the least subsequent office work compared to other methods requiring separate field-book reduction and plotting.
